## How to rename your branch from `master` to `main`

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- Many of you may have a default branch called `master` instead of `main`
- [This is completely fine!]{.alert} Both names work exactly the same way 👍
- GitHub changed the default branch name from `master` to `main` to use more inclusive language
- You can read more about the change [here](https://github.com/github/renaming)
- [You don't have to rename your branch]{.alert}, but if you want to, it's very easy! 😊
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
- To rename your current branch from `master` to `main`:

```bash
# Rename the branch locally
git branch -m master main

# Push the renamed branch to GitHub
git push -u origin main

# Delete the old master branch on GitHub
git push origin --delete master
```

- The `-m` flag stands for "move" (rename)
- After this, your default branch will be called `main`
- Remember to update any references to `master` in your workflows!
:::
:::
:::

# Pushing changes to a remote repository 🚀 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Pushing changes to a remote repository

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- Last class we learned to `add` and `commit`. Both stay on your machine
- To share your work, you need a [remote repository]{.alert}, usually on GitHub
- `git push` uploads your commits to it
- `git pull` downloads what other people have added
- That is the whole idea. The rest is detail
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/push-pull.png){width="150%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/push-pull.png"}
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Pushing changes to a remote repository

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 28px;"}
- Let's go back to our `my-project` local repository
- Check the last commit with `git log`
- Now, let's `push` our changes to a remote repository on GitHub
- First, we need to create a repository on GitHub
- Go to [GitHub](https://github.com) and click on the `+` sign on the top right corner
- Select `New repository`
- Name your repository `my-project`
- Click on `Create repository`
:::

## {background-image="figures/new-repo.png"}

## {background-image="figures/create-repo.png"}

## {background-image="figures/remote-repo.png"}

## Now, let's push our changes to GitHub

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 21px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- Why do we need to add a remote repository?
- Because we need to tell Git where to `push` our changes!
- `git remote add origin https://github.com/danilofreire/my-project.git`:
  - `remote`: tells Git we are adding a remote repository
  - `add`: adds a new remote repository
  - `origin`: the name of the remote repository
  -  `https://github.com/danilofreire/my-project.git` is the URL of the remote repository
- `git branch -M main`: makes sure the branch is called `main`
- `git push -u origin main`: pushes the changes, and remembers where to push next time
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/remote-add.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/remote-add.png"}
:::

- The `-u` flag sets the [upstream]{.alert}. After the first push, plain `git push` is enough
- If your branch is still called `master`, use that name instead. Everything works the same way
:::
:::
:::

# And voi-là! 🎉 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## {background-image="figures/push.png"}

## How to pull changes from a remote repository

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- To `push` further changes to the remote repository, you just repeat the process:
  - `git add file-name`
  - `git commit -m "Message"`
  - `git push` (no need to add the remote repository again)

- If you work by yourself on your computer only, [you already know everything you need to know about Git]{.alert} and you can go home now 😂
- Just kidding! There is still a lot to learn! 
- If you work with others, or if you use different computers, you need to know how to `pull` changes from GitHub
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
- To `pull` changes from a remote repository, use (you've guessed it) the command `git pull`
- `git pull` is the equivalent of `git fetch` + `git merge`
  - `git fetch` downloads the changes from the remote repository
  - `git merge` merges the changes with your local repository

- Let's see an example where I add a commit directly on GitHub
- I will add a [`.gitignore` file to ignore certain files and directories](https://docs.github.com/en/github/using-git/ignoring-files)
:::
:::
:::

## Adding `.gitignore` to our repository

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- On GitHub, I click `Add file` > `Create new file`, then commit
- `.gitignore` lists what Git should [never track]{.alert}:
  - By name: `secrets.txt`
  - By pattern: `*.csv` for every CSV
  - By folder: `data/`
- Use it for anything large, private, or regenerated: data, API keys, output
- Normally you would create this file [in the terminal]{.alert}. I am doing it on GitHub only so we have something to `pull` 😉
:::

:::

## Pulling changes 

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- Now, let's `pull` the changes to my local computer
- Just type `git pull` and the changes will be downloaded and merged
- If you work with others and they push changes to GitHub, you will need to `pull` the changes to your local computer too
:::

:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/pull.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/pull.png"}

## But wait a minute!

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- What if my coauthor and I change the same line?
- Different files, or different lines in the same file: Git merges them for you 👍
- The [same line]{.alert}: Git cannot guess which one you want, so it asks you
- This is a [merge conflict]{.alert}. It is normal, and it is not a disaster
- You resolve it by opening the file and choosing, or with a tool like `git mergetool`
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
- Let me change the `.gitignore` file both in my computer and on GitHub, and commit the changes (do not push yet)

## Resolving conflicts

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 21px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- To resolve the conflict, you need to open the file in a text editor
- You will see the changes from both you and your coauthor (or yourself)
- You can choose which changes to keep, or you can keep both changes
- After resolving the conflict, you need to `add` the file and `commit` the changes
- Then you can `push` the changes to GitHub

Git marks the conflict with three lines:

- `<<<<<<<` opens your version
- `=======` separates the two versions
- `>>>>>>>` closes their version, and names the commit it came from

Delete the markers along with the text you do not want
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/vim-conflict.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/vim-conflict.png"}
:::

- I will delete some lines and keep the changes from my computer
  
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/vim-conflict2.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/vim-conflict2.png"}
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Resolving conflicts

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- Now the conflict is resolved! 🥳

[![](figures/vim-conflict3.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/vim-conflict3.png"}
:::

- You can also use a graphical tool, such as [Sourcetree](https://www.sourcetreeapp.com) or [GitHub Desktop](https://desktop.github.com)

# Branches 🌿 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Branches

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- Branches are a way to work on different features or versions of your project
- The default branch is called `main` on GitHub, and `master` in older repositories
- However, you can create new branches to work on new features or versions [without affecting the `master` branch]{.alert}
- You can create a new branch with the command `git branch branch-name`
- And you can switch to the new branch with the command `git checkout branch-name`
  - Or you can use `git switch branch-name` if you have Git 2.23 or later
- You can also create a new branch and switch to it with the command `git checkout -b branch-name`
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/branches.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/branches.png"}
:::

- Branches may or may not be merged back to the `master` branch
- You can also delete branches after merging them
:::
:::
:::

## Branches

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- Let's create a new branch called `feature-1`
  - `git checkout -b feature-1`
- I will add a new file called `feature-1.txt` to the new branch
  - `echo "This is feature 1" > feature-1.txt`
- Then, I will `add`, `commit`, and `push` the changes to GitHub
  - `git add feature-1.txt && git commit -m "Add feature 1"`
  - `git push origin feature-1` (you need to push the new branch to GitHub)
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/branch.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/branch.png"}
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Branches

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- Now the branch is already on GitHub
- Let's merge the changes to the `master` branch
  - `git checkout master`
  - `git merge feature-1`
  - `git push`

- Done! Let's see what happened

- You can delete the branch with `git branch -d feature-1`
- To delete the branch on GitHub, use `git push origin --delete feature-1`
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/merge-branch.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/merge-branch.png"}

More about branches [here](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Branching-Branches-in-a-Nutshell).
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Going back to a specific commit

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="45%"}
- Find the commit first: `git log --oneline` lists the short hashes

Three ways back, from safest to most destructive:

- [Look around]{.alert}: `git checkout <hash>`. You are now in [detached HEAD]{.alert}, so anything you commit belongs to no branch
- [Keep your work]{.alert}: `git switch -c new-branch <hash>` starts a branch at that commit. Usually what you want
- [Move the branch itself]{.alert}: `git reset --hard <hash>` rewinds your branch and [throws away every commit after it]{.alert}

- `git switch main` brings you back to the present
:::

:::{.column width="55%"}
- Hashes are hexadecimal, so `0-9` and `a-f` only
- `a1b2c3d` is enough. The full form is 40 characters, like `470636f38e409f4f322c48183e19633ebb550625`
- Copy them, do not retype them
- Git keeps almost everything, so a lost commit can usually be recovered with `git reflog`
- On a shared project, branch rather than reset

:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/git-checkout.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/git-checkout.png"}
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Going back to a specific commit

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- `git switch -c` and `git checkout -b` do the same thing. `switch` is the newer, clearer name (Git 2.23+)
- `git branch -d branch-name` deletes a branch you have finished with
- `-D` forces the deletion, even when the work was never merged

:::{style="margin-top: 20px;"}
- [Rarely needed]{.alert}: replacing `main` altogether. Delete it, rename your current branch to `main`, then push
- [Never on a shared repository]{.alert}. Everyone else's work still points at the branch you deleted
:::
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/git-checkout2.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/git-checkout2.png"}
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Fork and clone 🍴 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Cloning

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="55%"}
- [Cloning]{.alert} downloads a repository from GitHub to your computer
- `git clone https://github.com/username/repository-name.git`
  - For instance, `git clone https://github.com/danilofreire/my-project.git`
- It creates a folder named after the repository
- Your copy stays [connected to the original]{.alert}
- So if the repository is not yours, [you cannot push to it]{.alert}
- Use it when you already have push rights and want to work locally
:::

:::{.column width="45%"}
- Cloning the `my-project` repository to a different folder

:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/clone.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/clone.png"}
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Forking

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- [Forking]{.alert} makes your own copy of a repository, [on your GitHub account]{.alert}
- Cloning copies to your computer. Forking copies to your account. That is the difference
- Because the fork is yours, [you can push to it]{.alert}
- It keeps a link back to the original, called the [upstream]{.alert} repository
- You can build something new from it, or [open a pull request]{.alert} to suggest changes back
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
[![](figures/fork.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/fork.png"}
:::
:::
:::

## Forking

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 28px;"}
- Forking from GitHub is easy, but it requires a few steps
- Forking [is not part of Git]{.alert}, but it is part of GitHub
  - That's why you cannot do it from the command line!
- To fork a repository, go to the repository on GitHub and click on the `Fork` button on the top right corner
- Then, you can clone your forked repository to your computer as you did before
:::

## Forking

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px; text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/fork-repo01.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/fork-repo01.png"}
:::

## Forking

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/fork-repo02.png){width="60%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/fork-repo02.png"}
:::

- After forking, you will see the repository on your GitHub account
- Clone it with `git clone https://github.com/your-username/repository-name.git`
:::

## Syncing a forked repository

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- A fork does not update itself. The original keeps moving without you
- [The easy way]{.alert}: on GitHub, click "Sync fork" and confirm. Commit your own work first
- [From the terminal]{.alert}, point at the original once, then pull from it whenever you like:

```bash
git remote add upstream https://github.com/original-user/original-repo.git
git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/main
git push
```

- `origin` is your fork. `upstream` is the repository you forked from
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
[![](figures/sync-fork.webp){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/sync-fork.webp"}

- More about syncing a forked repository [here](https://docs.github.com/en/github/collaborating-with-pull-requests/working-with-forks/syncing-a-fork).
:::
:::
:::

# Issues and pull requests 📥 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Issues and pull requests

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- [Issues]{.alert} are a way to track bugs, enhancements, or other tasks in a repository
- You can create an issue by clicking on the `Issues` tab on GitHub and then on the `New issue` button

:::{style="margin-top: 30px;"}
- [Pull requests]{.alert} are a way to suggest changes after you have forked and changed a repository
- You can create a pull request by clicking on the `Pull requests` tab on GitHub and then on the `New pull request` button
- The repository owner can then review your changes and merge them
- And that's how open-source projects work! 🤓🎉
:::
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}

# Other cool GitHub features 🌟🐙 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## GitHub has many other interesting features
### Gists

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- [Gists](https://gist.github.com) are a great way to share code snippets, notes, or other text
- You can create a Gist by clicking on the `+` sign on the top right corner of GitHub and then on `New gist`
- Paste any text or code and save it
- You can also create secret Gists that are not indexed by search engines
- Gists also benefit from version control, so you can see the history of changes and revert to previous versions
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/gist.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/gist.png"}
:::
:::
:::
:::

## GitHub Pages

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- This is one of the nicest features of GitHub
- [GitHub Pages](https://pages.github.com) allows you to create a website for your project, portfolio, or blog
- As you can see, I use GitHub Pages [for this course](https://danilofreire.github.io/datasci350) and [for my personal website](https://danilofreire.github.io)
- You can create a website by creating a new repository with the name `your-username.github.io`
- Then, you can upload your `.html`, `.css`, and `.js` files to the repository
- Your website will be available at `https://your-username.github.io`
- You can also use custom domains and [Jekyll themes](https://docs.github.com/en/pages/setting-up-a-github-pages-site-with-jekyll), which are pre-designed templates
- Available themes [here](https://pages.github.com/themes)
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/pages.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/pages.png"}
:::
:::
:::
:::

## GitHub Actions

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- [GitHub Actions](https://github.com/features/actions) runs code for you, on GitHub's machines
- You write a `.yml` file listing the steps. GitHub runs them whenever you push
- Typical uses: rebuild a website, run tests, train a model, publish a report
- It can also run on a schedule. Mine [rebuilds a list of my starred repositories every day](https://github.com/danilofreire/awesome-stars)
- The work happens on GitHub's machines, not yours, and public repositories get a generous free allowance
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/actions.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/actions.png"}
:::
:::
:::
:::

## GitHub Actions

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px; text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/actions2.png){width="82%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/actions2.png"}

## GitHub in the command line

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com/) is a command-line tool that brings GitHub to your terminal
- You can install it with `brew install gh`
- GitHub CLI creates repositories, issues, pull requests, and more
- I use it both to create repositories and clone/fork them
  - `gh repo create my-project`
  - `gh repo clone danilofreire/my-project`
- Have a look at the [GitHub CLI manual](https://cli.github.com/manual/) for more information
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/cli.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/cli.png"}

## Summary

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 26px;"}
- `git push` sends your commits to GitHub, `git pull` brings other people's back
- `.gitignore` keeps data, keys, and generated output out of the repository
- A [merge conflict]{.alert} means two people changed the same line. Git marks it, you choose
- [Branches]{.alert} let you work without touching `main`, and `merge` brings the work back
- `git switch -c new-branch <hash>` is the safe way to revisit an old commit
- [Clone]{.alert} copies a repository to your computer. [Fork]{.alert} copies it to your account
- [Issues]{.alert} track what needs doing, [pull requests]{.alert} propose the change itself
- Pages, Actions, Gists, and the CLI are all built on the same repository
:::

## Next class

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="55%"}
- [`git diff`]{.alert}: see exactly what changed, line by line, before you commit
- [Fixing mistakes]{.alert}: amend a commit message, and undo a commit with `git reset`
- [`git cherry-pick`]{.alert}: take one commit from a branch without merging the whole thing
- [`git rebase`]{.alert}: replay your commits on top of someone else's work
- Plus more of the GitHub CLI
- Bring your `my-project` repository. We will keep working on it 🤓
